characters: Kwadwo: a 12-year-old boy in a white shirt and brown shorts, holding a bundle of thin sticks.
Esther: his classmate, 12, in a school uniform with plaits, taking notes.
Mr Anim: their history teacher, in a kente-print shirt, holding up a single stick.
The Asante union: a story picture of several chiefs standing together in front of a stool.

narrationPlan.voice: Strong, steady teacher’s voice for Mr Anim; eager young voices for Kwadwo and Esther
narrationPlan.pace: Strong and clear, slowing at the dates (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Strong talking drums building slowly, with a steady, proud rhythm (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The Asante union is a major part of Ghana’s history. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils. The Golden Stool is sacred; the story refers to it briefly and with respect.
The saying about one stick and a bundle is told in many parts of Africa and is used here as a classroom teaching device, not as a quotation from a particular source.
The meaning of the name Asante is told as an explanation people give, not as settled fact.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: Denkyira dominance in the late 1600s; Osei Tutu and Okomfo Anokye; Feyiase as the decisive battle; Ntim Gyakari killed; the cannons; the date given as August 1701 by one source and 1700 by another; Odwira; expansion between 1700 and 1750.
Have Asante cultural authorities, Manhyia or an Asante history teacher review the wording, especially about the Golden Stool and the origin of the name.
The number of captured cannons is unclear in sources and is not stated; keep it out.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about unity and about how historians work. It teaches how small states joined against a larger power, why symbols matter and why two sources can give different dates.
learningGoals: Explain why the states joined together and how.
Describe the union’s symbols and rules.
Compare two dates for the same event and explain why they might differ.

subjectLinks.subject: Social Studies / History
subjectLinks.link: Kingdoms and unions before colonial rule

beforeReading: Do the stick demonstration with learners before reading.
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to write both dates and give two reasons they might differ.
afterReading: Make a bundle of sticks or straws and explain the lesson to a partner.
Write a short speech urging cooperation, in the voice of a leader at the union’s founding.
discussion: Why was a shared symbol important?
What can go wrong in a union, and how can leaders prevent it?
reflection: How can your class become like a bundle?

mathsExtension.task: If Feyiase was in 1700, how many years ago was it from 2026? And if 1701?
The union expanded between 1700 and 1750. How many years is that?

support: Give learners a two-column chart: What we know / What we are unsure about.
stretch: Find out how the Asante later organised their army and government.

culturalNotes: The Asante union is a major part of Ghana’s history. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils. The Golden Stool is sacred; the story refers to it briefly and with respect.
The saying about one stick and a bundle is told in many parts of Africa and is used here as a classroom teaching device, not as a quotation from a particular source.
The meaning of the name Asante is told as an explanation people give, not as settled fact.
localiseThis: Invite a local historian or a member of the community to speak.
Follow local custom when speaking about chiefs and the Golden Stool.

whatWeKnow: Denkyira dominated its neighbours in the late 1600s and was defeated by the Asante union at Feyiase.
The Golden Stool became a symbol of unity.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact year of Feyiase, which one source gives as August 1701 and another as 1700.
The details of how Denkyira’s king died, which accounts describe differently.

factCheck.claim: Osei Tutu and Okomfo Anokye founded the Asante kingdom around the end of the 17th century; Denkyira conquered neighbouring kingdoms in the last decade of the century; the union’s victory at Feyiase in 1700 ended Denkyira rule; the Golden Stool is the seal of the union; Odwira and a politico-military constitution were set up; between 1700 and 1750 the union grew to cover an area larger than modern Ghana.
factCheck.explanation: From the Manhyia Palace Archives’ account of the Asante union, which says Anokye “is believed” to have called the stool and gives many dates as approximate.
factCheck.reference: Manhyia Palace Museum / Archives, “History of Asante Union”.

factCheck.claim: The Battle of Feyiase took place in August 1701 between the Asante (under Osei Tutu) and Denkyira (under Ntim Gyakari); Denkyira had a few Dutch cannons; Ntim Gyakari was killed; the Asante captured the cannons.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s article on the battle, which cites academic sources and notes uncertainty about the cannon count and the account of the king’s death.
